grading: An eval passes iff ALL must_pass assertions hold AND >= 80% of scored assertions hold. must_pass assertions are necessary conditions — they catch over-application, outright errors, and acceptance of false premises. scored assertions capture core correctness; a response earns credit if it clearly demonstrates the described behavior.
notes: Evals probe the behaviors the skill is meant to produce: asymptotic-robustness reasoning, correct estimand interpretation, GLM family selection, refusal to assumption-police, robustness-vs-exactness judgment, and nuanced practical advice. Crucially they also test the inverse failure mode — over-application — with cases where the correct response is short and the simple method is right (evals 16, 17). Each eval has assertions phrased as objectively checkable statements about the response. Several evals are deliberately ambiguous or have multiple defensible answers; their assertions reward acknowledging that rather than asserting one verdict. A few assertions name a specific method only as an example ('e.g. ...') — grade the reasoning, not the keyword, and accept equivalent correct approaches.

evals.prompt: I have two groups, about 80 people each, and I want to compare their average monthly spend. The data are right-skewed and a Shapiro-Wilk test on each group rejects normality (p < .001). Can I still use a t-test, or do I have to switch to Mann-Whitney?
evals.expected_output: Explains that the t-test concerns the sampling distribution of the mean, not the raw data; with n~80/group and only moderate skew the CLT makes the t-test approximately valid; Shapiro-Wilk rejection at this n is expected and not decisive; recommends Welch's t-test; notes Mann-Whitney answers a different question (stochastic ordering, not difference in means) unless a location-shift is assumed; possibly distinguishes whether the mean or median is the intended estimand.

assertions.text: States or implies the relevant object is the sampling distribution of the mean, not the distribution of the raw data
Says the t-test is approximately valid / okay here given n~80 per group (does not forbid it)
Notes that Shapiro-Wilk rejecting at this sample size is uninformative or expected, and does not treat it as a decisive gate
Recommends or mentions Welch's t-test (or otherwise addresses unequal variances) rather than the equal-variance pretest
Notes that Mann-Whitney tests stochastic ordering / P(X>Y), not equality of means or medians in general (location-shift caveat)
Does NOT mechanically conclude 'normality rejected therefore use a nonparametric test'

evals.prompt: My sample is huge (2.3 million rows). Does that mean I don't have to worry about my regression assumptions anymore?
evals.expected_output: Distinguishes what large N does and does not fix. Large N makes the CLT-based level of tests accurate and shrinks approximation error, but does NOT fix dependence/clustering, confounding/identification, model misspecification (bias in the mean structure), or the fact that everything becomes statistically significant so effect sizes matter. Notes assumption tests will reject everything at this n.

assertions.text: States that large N helps with the level/normal-approximation of tests (CLT) but does not fix everything
Names at least two things large N does NOT fix from: dependence/clustering, confounding/identification, model/mean misspecification, wrong estimand
Notes that at this N nearly everything is statistically significant and effect sizes / intervals matter more than p-values
Does NOT claim that large N makes assumptions irrelevant wholesale

evals.prompt: I'm modeling the number of support tickets each customer files per month. Should I use Poisson or negative binomial regression?
evals.expected_output: Frames the choice around the mean-variance relationship. Poisson assumes variance = mean (equidispersion); ticket counts are typically overdispersed, so NB (quadratic variance) or quasi-Poisson (linear variance) is usually the right call. Explains how to check (dispersion ratio / variance-vs-mean plot), that overdispersion deflates Poisson SEs rather than biasing coefficients, and mentions an offset for exposure if applicable. May mention NB vs quasi-Poisson differ in variance shape.

assertions.text: Frames the decision around the mean-variance relationship / equidispersion vs overdispersion
Notes that count data like this are usually overdispersed and therefore NB or quasi-Poisson is typically preferred over plain Poisson
Explains how to detect overdispersion (dispersion statistic relative to df, or variance-vs-mean plot)
States that overdispersion mainly deflates the standard errors rather than biasing the point estimates (if the mean model is right)
Mentions at least one of: offset for exposure, NB-vs-quasi-Poisson variance shape difference, or checking excess zeros

evals.prompt: We ran a randomized A/B test on checkout flow. Someone on my team says we need to control for device type, browser, and whether the user completed onboarding, since those differ a bit between the two arms. Should I add those as covariates?
evals.expected_output: Because it's randomized, the unadjusted difference is already unbiased for the causal effect; covariate adjustment is for precision, not bias. Pre-specified pre-treatment covariates (device, browser) can be adjusted for to gain precision. BUT 'completed onboarding' is plausibly post-treatment/affected by the arm, and controlling for it would induce bias (post-treatment / mediator / collider). Small chance imbalances in an RCT are expected and not a reason to fear bias.

assertions.text: States that in a randomized experiment the unadjusted difference is already unbiased for the causal effect and adjustment is mainly for precision
Flags that 'completed onboarding' may be post-treatment / a mediator or collider and that controlling for it can introduce bias
Distinguishes pre-treatment covariates (okay to adjust, ideally pre-specified) from post-treatment variables (do not adjust)
Notes that small covariate imbalances under randomization are expected and not evidence of confounding
Does NOT advise blindly adding all three covariates as 'more rigorous'

evals.prompt: My residuals aren't normal (clear deviation in the QQ plot) and there's some funneling. The model is an OLS of revenue on a handful of predictors, n=400. Walk me through what to do.
evals.expected_output: Triages: funneling = heteroskedasticity (affects SEs, not coefficient bias) -> use HC3 robust SEs. Non-normal residuals at n=400 matter little for coefficient inference (CLT) but check for the more important issue: is the non-normality a symptom of a misspecified mean (nonlinearity, missing terms, wrong scale)? Look at residuals-vs-fitted for curvature. Considers whether revenue's skew/positivity suggests a GLM (gamma/log) if that's the generative structure. Avoids reflexively transforming just to normalize residuals.

assertions.text: Identifies funneling as heteroskedasticity and recommends heteroskedasticity-robust (sandwich/HC, ideally HC3) standard errors
States that heteroskedasticity affects the standard errors, not the unbiasedness of the OLS coefficients
Notes that non-normal residuals at n=400 are of limited concern for coefficient inference due to the CLT
Recommends checking whether the residual pattern signals a misspecified mean structure (nonlinearity / omitted terms) rather than only a distributional issue
Mentions that a GLM (e.g. gamma/log) may fit revenue's generative structure better, OR cautions against transforming purely to normalize residuals (changing the estimand)

evals.prompt: I want to report the difference in median household income between two neighborhoods. A colleague says just use a t-test. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: The estimand is the median, but a t-test targets the mean. This is an estimand mismatch, not an assumption issue. To target the median, use median/quantile regression or report medians with an appropriate CI (bootstrap). Mann-Whitney is about stochastic ordering, not the median difference unless location-shift holds. If the mean were actually the target, the t-test could be fine despite skew at adequate n.

assertions.text: Identifies that the question is about the median (the estimand) while a t-test targets the mean
Frames this primarily as an estimand mismatch rather than an assumption violation
Suggests a method that actually targets the median (quantile/median regression, or bootstrap CI for the median difference)
Notes that Mann-Whitney does not directly estimate the median difference unless a location-shift assumption holds
Does NOT simply endorse the t-test as a test of medians

evals.prompt: My logistic regression has one coefficient that came back as 14.2 with a standard error of 3400. What's going on and how do I fix it?
evals.expected_output: Classic complete/quasi-complete separation: the predictor (or a combination) perfectly or nearly perfectly predicts the outcome, so the MLE diverges, giving a huge estimate and enormous SE. Fix with penalization (Firth) or weakly-informative Bayesian priors; check for sparse cells. Not a normality/multicollinearity issue.

assertions.text: Diagnoses (quasi-)complete separation as the cause of the huge coefficient and enormous SE
Explains that under separation the MLE diverges / has no finite maximum
Recommends a fix such as Firth penalized logistic regression or weakly-informative Bayesian priors
Mentions checking for sparse / small cell counts or a near-perfect predictor
Does NOT misattribute the symptom to multicollinearity or non-normality

evals.prompt: A reviewer is demanding I drop variables because my VIFs are above 5. I care about the coefficient on price, which has a VIF of 2.1. The high-VIF variables are control variables I'm not interpreting. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Multicollinearity inflates SEs of the collinear coefficients but biases nothing and doesn't affect coefficients outside the collinear set. Since price's VIF is low and the high-VIF variables are controls not being interpreted, the collinearity is largely irrelevant to the estimand of interest; dropping controls could introduce omitted-variable bias. Pushes back on reflexive VIF-dropping. Could offer to explain this to the reviewer.

assertions.text: States that multicollinearity inflates standard errors of the collinear coefficients but does not bias estimates
Notes that collinearity among controls does not impair the coefficient of interest (price) when price itself is not highly collinear
Warns that dropping the control variables could introduce omitted-variable bias
Pushes back on the reflexive 'VIF > 5 so drop variables' rule rather than complying with it
Frames the decision in terms of the goal/estimand (the price coefficient) rather than a mechanical threshold

evals.prompt: I have data from 6 hospitals, with hundreds of patients each, and treatment was assigned at the hospital level. I clustered my standard errors by hospital. Is that enough?
evals.expected_output: Clustering at the hospital level is the right level, but with only 6 clusters cluster-robust SEs are biased downward and over-reject; the asymptotics are in the number of clusters, not patients. Hundreds of patients per cluster does not help. Recommends wild cluster bootstrap or small-cluster corrections, and notes the fundamental limitation of so few clusters for inference. Treatment assigned at cluster level also raises the broader design point.

assertions.text: States that the relevant asymptotics are in the number of clusters, not the number of patients, so hundreds per cluster does not rescue inference
Identifies 6 clusters as too few for standard cluster-robust SEs (downward bias / over-rejection)

Recommends an appropriate response to few clusters (e.g. wild cluster bootstrap, a small-cluster degrees-of-freedom correction, or design-based inference) or at minimum flags that standard cluster-robust SEs are unreliable with so few clusters
Confirms hospital is the appropriate clustering level given treatment was assigned at that level
Does NOT say that clustering by hospital with large per-hospital n is sufficient

evals.prompt: Should I model my outcome (proportion of a budget spent on category X, between 0 and 1) with logistic regression?
evals.expected_output: Logistic regression is for Bernoulli/binomial outcomes (counts of successes out of trials), not for a continuous proportion in (0,1) that isn't a success count. Beta regression is the natural choice for a continuous bounded proportion. If the proportion is actually k successes out of n known trials, binomial/logistic is appropriate. Note handling of exact 0s/1s (zero/one-inflated beta or transformation). A fractional-logit (quasi-binomial) GLM is also a defensible option.

assertions.text: Distinguishes a continuous proportion in (0,1) from a count of successes out of trials
Recommends beta regression (or fractional/quasi-binomial logit) for a continuous bounded proportion
Says plain logistic regression is appropriate when the outcome is successes out of a known number of trials
Mentions handling exact 0s and 1s (e.g. zero/one-inflated beta or a transformation) if beta regression is used
Does NOT simply endorse logistic regression without qualification

evals.prompt: I'm comparing pre/post test scores for a treatment and control group that were NOT randomized. Should I analyze change scores (post minus pre) or run ANCOVA controlling for the pre-test? I got different answers from each.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes Lord's paradox: in non-randomized pre/post data, change-score and ANCOVA target different estimands and can legitimately disagree. The right choice depends on the causal model and assignment mechanism (does conditioning on baseline close a confounding path or open a collider / induce regression-to-the-mean artifacts?). There is no purely statistical resolution; should make the causal assumptions explicit. Under randomization ANCOVA would be preferred for efficiency, but it's not randomized here.

assertions.text: Names or describes Lord's paradox / that the two methods target different estimands and can legitimately disagree
States that the choice depends on the causal model and assignment mechanism, not a purely statistical rule
Explains the difference in what each estimates (amount of change vs follow-up adjusted for baseline)
Notes that because it is non-randomized, there is no purely statistical resolution and the causal assumptions must be made explicit
Avoids declaring one method universally correct without reference to the causal question

evals.prompt: My costs data are very right-skewed and positive. My instinct is to log-transform and run OLS. A colleague says use a gamma GLM with a log link. Does it matter which?
evals.expected_output: Yes, it matters because they target different estimands: log-OLS estimates E[log Y] (exponentiating gives the geometric mean, ~median-ish), while gamma-with-log-link estimates log E[Y] (the arithmetic mean). Retransformation/Jensen bias means you can't naively exponentiate log-OLS fitted values to get E[Y]; a smearing correction is needed and depends on the error variance (problematic under heteroskedasticity). Choice depends on whether you want effects on the arithmetic mean (gamma) or the multiplicative/geometric-mean scale (log-OLS). Both are defensible; name the estimand.

assertions.text: States that log-OLS estimates E[log Y] (geometric mean upon exponentiation) while gamma-log estimates log E[Y] (arithmetic mean) — i.e. different estimands
Explains the retransformation / Jensen's inequality problem with naively exponentiating log-OLS predictions to recover E[Y]
Notes the retransformation correction (smearing) depends on the error variance and is complicated by heteroskedasticity
Frames the decision as which estimand/scale you want rather than which is 'more correct'
Treats both as defensible rather than dismissing one outright

evals.prompt: Is it valid to use linear regression on a binary outcome (the linear probability model)? Someone told me it is always wrong to use LPM and you must use logistic regression instead.
evals.expected_output: Declines the pure yes/no and gives nuance: the LPM gives consistent estimates of marginal effects / risk differences and is popular in econometrics, but has drawbacks (predictions outside [0,1], inherent heteroskedasticity -> use robust SEs, nonlinearity near the bounds). It's defensible when the estimand is the average marginal effect / risk difference and probabilities are away from 0/1; logistic is better when you need valid probabilities or odds ratios or have extreme probabilities. Multiple approaches defensible depending on estimand.

assertions.text: Declines to give a bare yes/no and explains why the answer is conditional
Notes legitimate uses of the LPM (interpretable marginal effects / risk differences; common in applied econometrics)
Notes drawbacks: predictions can fall outside [0,1], built-in heteroskedasticity requiring robust SEs, poor behavior near the bounds
Ties the choice to the estimand (risk difference / marginal effect vs probabilities / odds ratios)
Presents both LPM and logistic as defensible depending on the goal rather than declaring one always correct

evals.prompt: My count outcome has a ton of zeros (about 60% zeros). I read that I need a zero-inflated model. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: Not necessarily. First check whether a negative binomial already accommodates the zeros (NB can absorb substantial zero excess). Choose between hurdle and zero-inflated based on the data-generating story: hurdle = one zero process (truncated count for positives + binary for any), zero-inflated = a structural-zero class plus a count process that can also produce zeros (two routes to zero). The decision should be substantive (are there 'never at risk' units distinct from incidental zeros?), not driven by the zero proportion alone. Compare via posterior predictive / fit on the zero count.

assertions.text: Says a zero-inflated model is not automatically required and recommends first checking whether negative binomial absorbs the zeros
Distinguishes hurdle (single zero process) from zero-inflated (structural zeros plus a count process that also yields zeros)
Frames the choice around the substantive data-generating story (e.g. 'never at risk' structural zeros vs incidental zeros) rather than the zero percentage alone
Mentions checking model adequacy on the zeros (e.g. posterior predictive / comparing observed vs predicted zero counts)
Does NOT reflexively prescribe zero-inflation just because there are many zeros

evals.prompt: Before every analysis I run normality tests, Levene's test, and Breusch-Pagan, and I pick my method based on the results. Is this a good workflow?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the pretest-and-switch workflow. Assumption tests answer 'is the assumption exactly true' (always no) not 'is the violation consequential'; underpowered at small n, overpowered at large n; and pretesting distorts the operating characteristics (level/coverage) of the final inference. Better: reason about robustness directly, use robust-by-design methods (Welch, HC3/robust SEs, appropriate GLM), and use graphical diagnostics to judge magnitude. Not a mechanical check-then-choose pipeline.

assertions.text: Pushes back on the test-then-choose workflow rather than endorsing it
Explains that assumption tests check exact truth, not whether the violation is consequential, and are underpowered at small n / overpowered at large n
Notes that pretesting distorts the level/coverage of the final inference (pretest bias)
Recommends robust-by-design methods (e.g. Welch, robust/HC SEs, appropriate model family) and/or graphical diagnostics for magnitude instead
Frames good practice as reasoning about consequences for the estimand/goal rather than a mechanical pipeline

evals.prompt: We ran a clean randomized experiment, ~6,000 users per arm, comparing average session length (in minutes). The distribution is a bit right-skewed. I just want to know if the new design increased average session length. Is a t-test fine or do I need something fancier?
evals.expected_output: Short answer: a t-test (Welch) is fine, and the simple difference in means is the unbiased causal effect because of randomization. With ~6,000/arm the CLT handles the mild skew for inference about the mean. No transformation, GLM, or nonparametric switch is warranted. A good response is brief and confident, does not invent estimand subtleties, and at most mentions reporting the effect size/CI and using Welch.

assertions.text: Says a (Welch) t-test / difference in means is fine here without hedging
Notes that randomization makes the simple difference in means the unbiased causal effect
Notes that the large per-arm n handles the mild skew via the CLT
Does NOT recommend a transformation, GLM, or nonparametric test for this case
Does NOT manufacture unnecessary estimand or robustness caveats; the response is proportionate and largely affirming

evals.prompt: n = 300 in each of two independent groups, outcome roughly symmetric, I want to compare means. Anything I actually need to worry about before running a two-sample t-test?
evals.expected_output: Essentially no — with n=300/group and symmetric data the t-test is on very solid ground. The only worthwhile notes: use Welch by default (don't bother with an equal-variance pretest), look at whether a couple of influential points drive things, and confirm independence. Should be brief and reassuring, not a catalogue of diagnostics.

assertions.text: Reassures that the t-test is fine / there is little to worry about given n=300 and symmetry
Mentions Welch as the sensible default and/or that an equal-variance pretest is unnecessary
Keeps the response brief and proportionate rather than enumerating many diagnostics or alternative methods
Does NOT invoke normality tests as a gate or recommend a nonparametric switch

evals.prompt: I have 500,000 rows. The outcome is a count (number of purchases in a window) and I just want the average difference between two cohorts. Do I have to use a Poisson or negative binomial model, or can I just use OLS / a t-test on the counts?
evals.expected_output: Distinguishes goals. For inference about the difference in MEAN counts, OLS with robust (HC) SEs (or a t-test) is consistent and valid even though the outcome is a count — the CLT covers it, and at n=500k it is rock solid. You do NOT need a GLM for validity. The GLM is the right tool if you instead want a rate ratio / multiplicative effect (its more natural estimand), in-bounds predictions, or efficiency — but at this n efficiency matters little, and a linear-scale mean difference is interpretable and collapsible. So: name the estimand. Additive mean difference -> OLS+robust SE is fine; rate ratio / predictions -> Poisson/NB (NB if overdispersed).

assertions.text: States that for the difference in mean counts, OLS+robust SEs (or a t-test) is valid here and a GLM is not required for validity
Attributes that validity to the CLT / large n rather than to the outcome being normal
Identifies what a Poisson/NB model actually adds: a multiplicative/rate-ratio estimand, in-bounds predictions, and/or efficiency — not validity
Notes the choice hinges on the estimand (additive mean difference vs rate ratio) rather than on a rule that counts 'require' a count model
Mentions that at this very large n the efficiency advantage of the GLM is small
Does NOT assert that count outcomes must be modeled with Poisson/NB

evals.prompt: I have a small, heavy-tailed sample (n=40) and I want a confidence interval for the maximum value the process can produce. I'll just bootstrap the maximum — that's assumption-free, right?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back: the nonparametric bootstrap is NOT assumption-free and specifically FAILS for the maximum (and other extreme order statistics) — the bootstrap distribution of the max does not converge to the right thing because the statistic is non-smooth and pinned to observed extremes. Heavy tails and small n make it worse. Appropriate tools: extreme-value theory (fit a GEV / use the generalized Pareto over a threshold), or m-out-of-n / subsampling bootstrap which can be consistent where the naive bootstrap isn't. General point: the bootstrap inherits assumptions (iid resampling, smooth functional, finite-variance-friendly).

assertions.text: States that the naive bootstrap is not assumption-free and fails (is inconsistent) for the maximum / extreme order statistics
Explains why: the maximum is a non-smooth functional pinned to the observed extreme, so the bootstrap distribution doesn't converge correctly
Notes that small n and heavy tails make estimating an extreme quantity especially fragile
Recommends a more appropriate approach (extreme-value theory / GEV / peaks-over-threshold, or m-out-of-n / subsampling)
Does NOT endorse the plan as a valid assumption-free procedure

evals.prompt: My churn-prediction model has an AUC of 0.86. Stakeholders want to use the predicted probabilities to prioritize retention spend. Is the model good enough?
evals.expected_output: Distinguishes discrimination from calibration. AUC measures ranking/discrimination only; it says nothing about whether the predicted probabilities are correct in magnitude. Because the probabilities will be used to allocate spend (a decision based on probability magnitude / expected value), CALIBRATION is what matters and AUC alone doesn't establish it. Recommend a calibration/reliability plot (predicted vs observed frequency) and recalibration (Platt/isotonic) if miscalibrated; also note the decision may need expected-value/threshold analysis, not just a good AUC.

assertions.text: Distinguishes discrimination (AUC/ranking) from calibration (probabilities correct in magnitude)
States that AUC alone does not establish that the predicted probabilities are trustworthy
Notes that because the probabilities drive a spending/decision, calibration is the property that matters here
Recommends checking calibration (reliability/calibration plot) and recalibrating (e.g. Platt/isotonic) if needed
Does NOT declare the model adequate for the decision on the basis of AUC alone

evals.prompt: Here's my Poisson regression output for daily complaint counts. Coefficients look reasonable and several are highly significant (p < 0.001). Residual deviance = 4,812 on 1,180 degrees of freedom. Is this model good to report?
evals.expected_output: Spots overdispersion: deviance/df = 4812/1180 ~ 4.1, far above 1, signaling strong overdispersion. Consequence: Poisson coefficients may be fine but the SEs are too small and the p < 0.001 values are over-optimistic — significance is likely overstated. Recommend refitting with negative binomial or quasi-Poisson, or using robust/cluster SEs, then re-checking which effects survive. Also suggests checking the variance-vs-mean pattern and excess zeros / offset for exposure.

assertions.text: Computes or notes the dispersion ratio (deviance/df ~ 4) and identifies substantial overdispersion
States that under overdispersion the Poisson coefficients may be okay but the SEs are too small and the reported p-values are over-optimistic
Warns that the highly-significant results may not survive once dispersion is handled
Recommends negative binomial or quasi-Poisson, or robust SEs, as the fix
Does NOT accept the model as report-ready on the basis of significance alone

evals.prompt: I ran the same regression in men and women separately. In men the coefficient on treatment is 0.42 (p = 0.03). In women it's 0.31 (p = 0.12). So the treatment effect is significant in men but not women — that means the treatment works differently by sex, right?
evals.expected_output: No. 'Significant in one group, not the other' is not a valid test of whether the effects differ. The correct test is a direct contrast or interaction term (treatment × sex) in a joint model. The two estimates and their CIs likely overlap substantially. Under independence, the SE of the difference is √(SE₁² + SE₂²), and the difference 0.42 − 0.31 = 0.11 may be nowhere near significant. This is the difference-in-significance fallacy (Gelman & Stern 2006).

assertions.text: States that 'significant in one group, not the other' does NOT establish that the effects differ between groups
States the correct test is a direct contrast or interaction term (treatment × sex / group), not a comparison of individual p-values
Explains why: two effects can each be (non-)significant individually while their difference has a different significance status
Notes or implies the SE of the difference is larger than either individual SE (e.g. √(SE₁² + SE₂²) under independence)
Does NOT accept the subgroup p-value comparison as a valid test of the between-group difference

evals.prompt: We ran a small pilot study — 9 people per group, so n=18 total — and found d = 0.9, p = 0.04. The effect is large and significant! This is great news for the intervention, right?
evals.expected_output: Red flag, not reassurance. With n=18 the study has low power; significant estimates at low power systematically overstate the true effect (Type M error / exaggeration ratio). The observed d=0.9 is likely a substantial overestimate of the true effect. Non-trivial Type S risk also applies: a fraction of significant estimates at this power level are the wrong sign. 'Large and significant from a tiny study' is the winner's curse. Treat as preliminary; more data needed.

assertions.text: Flags low power as a concern — n=18 is a very small sample for an effect of this magnitude
Names or describes the Type M / exaggeration ratio concern: significant estimates from low-powered studies systematically overstate the true effect
Notes that at low power the true effect could be much smaller, negligible, or even in the wrong direction — the observed large effect is not trustworthy at face value
Recommends treating the result as preliminary / hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive
Does NOT simply validate 'large and significant' as strong confirmation of the intervention's efficacy

evals.prompt: I fit a logistic regression for stroke (1/0) with the main exposure being hypertension, and I also included age, sex, smoking, and diabetes as covariates. My Table 2 reports all five coefficients with p-values, and I'm interpreting each as 'the effect of that variable on stroke risk.' Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No — this is the Table 2 fallacy. The model was built to estimate the effect of hypertension; the other variables were included as confounders for that estimand. Each covariate's coefficient is conditional on all other terms, adjusted for hypertension's confounders (not necessarily each covariate's own confounders). Some covariates may be mediators of others; the adjustment set may be wrong for their individual causal effects. Only the pre-specified estimand (hypertension → stroke) is interpretable as a causal effect; the others are not their total causal effects.

assertions.text: Identifies the Table 2 fallacy or equivalent concern: covariate coefficients in a multivariable model do not each estimate their own total causal effect
Explains that each coefficient is conditional on all others and subject to different confounding than the main exposure
Notes the model was designed to estimate one estimand (hypertension → stroke); other coefficients are incidental to that design
Warns that some covariates may be mediators of others, making their coefficients further uninterpretable as total causal effects
Does NOT endorse reporting all coefficients as causal effects of each variable without qualification

evals.prompt: I had 15 candidate predictors. I ran backward stepwise selection (dropping variables by p-value > 0.10) and ended up with 6 in the final model. I'm now reporting the coefficients and p-values from that final model. Is this a valid inference procedure?
evals.expected_output: No — this is post-selection inference. The p-values and CIs in the stepwise-selected model do not have their nominal meaning; the selection process consumed degrees of freedom that the final analysis pretends it had, making the reported p-values anti-conservative. This is the pretest-bias problem generalized to model selection. Mitigations: pre-register the analysis, use a held-out test set for confirmatory inference, use selective inference methods, or label results as exploratory/hypothesis-generating.

assertions.text: States that reporting p-values from a model selected by the same data is invalid / anti-conservative (post-selection inference problem)
Explains that the stepwise selection process distorts the nominal meaning of the final model's p-values
Notes that the inflation of false positives comes from the implicit search across models, not only from explicitly running the same test many times
Recommends at least one mitigation: pre-registration, sample splitting, honest exploratory labeling, or selective inference methods
Does NOT endorse the reported p-values as having their nominal meaning

evals.prompt: About 20% of my observations are missing on the outcome variable. I'm planning to just drop them and do complete-case analysis. Walk me through when that's okay and when it's not.
evals.expected_output: Complete-case validity depends on the missing data mechanism. MCAR → complete-case is unbiased but inefficient (20% loss is non-trivial). MAR: if outcome missingness depends only on covariates included in the model (not on the unobserved outcome itself given those covariates), complete-case regression coefficients can be unbiased — this is an important subtlety. MNAR → complete-case is biased; no data-only fix. With 20% missing, should investigate what predicts missingness and consider multiple imputation under MAR or sensitivity analysis under MNAR.

assertions.text: States that complete-case validity depends on the missingness mechanism (MCAR / MAR / MNAR)
Correctly states MCAR → complete-case is unbiased (though inefficient)
States the MAR subtlety: complete-case is valid for regression coefficients when outcome missingness depends only on covariates in the model, not on the unobserved outcome given those covariates
States that MNAR → complete-case is biased and cannot be fixed from data alone; requires sensitivity analysis or explicit MNAR modeling
Does NOT simply endorse dropping the 20% without qualification or mention of the missingness mechanism

evals.prompt: I'm studying how a job training program affects wages. I suspect the effect might be different for people at the bottom of the wage distribution than for those in the middle or top. OLS gives me an average effect. What should I use instead?
evals.expected_output: Quantile regression. It models the conditional quantile (e.g. 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th percentile) of wages given the predictors, giving a separate coefficient at each quantile. This directly answers the question: does training affect low earners differently than high earners? Unlike OLS, it reveals heterogeneous effects across the distribution rather than averaging them. No parametric distributional assumption on the errors is needed; inference via bootstrap or asymptotic theory.

assertions.text: Recommends quantile regression as the appropriate method for this question
Explains that quantile regression models the conditional quantile (not the conditional mean) at specified percentiles
Notes it reveals heterogeneous effects across the distribution that OLS would average away
Notes that no parametric distributional assumption on the errors is needed (distribution-free in that sense)
Does NOT recommend only OLS or treating the average effect as sufficient for this distributional question

evals.prompt: I have a randomized experiment comparing two groups, but the outcome has a weird, heavy-tailed distribution. Someone suggests a permutation test because it's 'assumption-free.' Is that right, and what exactly does a permutation test test?
evals.expected_output: A permutation test is well-suited here, but it is not entirely assumption-free — it requires exchangeability under the null. In a randomized experiment, exchangeability holds by design, which is exactly why permutation tests are natural here. What the test tests is the sharp null of no effect for any unit — a stronger statement than equality of means. It gives exact finite-sample Type I error control without distributional assumptions. The distributional weirdness is handled; the relevant nuance is the sharp vs weak null distinction.

assertions.text: States that exchangeability (from the randomization) is the key assumption justifying the permutation test, not that it is entirely assumption-free
States that the null being tested is the sharp null (no effect for any unit), which is stronger than equality of means
Notes that distributional assumptions (normality, etc.) are not needed and exact Type I error control holds in finite samples
Notes at least one limitation or nuance: e.g. sensitivity to variance differences under heterogeneous effects, or the sharp vs composite null distinction
Does NOT claim the permutation test is entirely assumption-free

evals.prompt: Everyone knows you must log-transform right-skewed data before running a regression. My revenue outcome is skewed, so I'll log it first. That's the right move, right?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back: the premise is incorrect — log-transformation is not universally required before regression on skewed data. Log-transforming changes the estimand: OLS on log(Y) targets E[log Y] (geometric-mean-scale effects), not E[Y] (arithmetic mean effects). If you want effects on the arithmetic mean, log-transforming gives the wrong answer. For mean-contrast inference, CLT handles moderate skewness at adequate n without transformation. If multiplicative effects are the right estimand, log-OLS is defensible — but that is an estimand choice, not an assumption fix.

assertions.text: Does NOT accept the false premise that log-transformation is universally required before regression on skewed data
Explains that log-transforming changes the estimand (from effects on E[Y] / arithmetic mean to effects on E[log Y] / geometric mean)
Notes that raw-data skewness is not automatically a problem for OLS at adequate n — the relevant question is the sampling distribution of the estimator
Response is proportionate and corrects the premise concisely without a lengthy lecture
Does NOT recommend log-transforming without first identifying what estimand the user actually wants

evals.prompt: My sample size is 150 per group, and the histogram looks clearly non-normal — there's skew and the tails are fat. That means I definitely can't use a t-test here. Right?
evals.expected_output: No — this is the central misconception the skill addresses. The t-test does not assume raw-data normality; it assumes the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal, which the CLT delivers at n=150 per group for virtually all distributions with finite variance. A non-normal histogram is the wrong thing to look at. At n=150 the t-test is almost certainly fine for inference about the mean. Heavy tails reduce efficiency but not the level of the test. The decision should rest on the estimand and n relative to skew, not on the histogram shape.

assertions.text: Does NOT accept the false premise that non-normal raw data prohibits using a t-test
States the relevant object is the sampling distribution of the mean (not the raw data distribution), governed by the CLT
Affirms that at n=150 per group the t-test is approximately valid for inference about the mean despite non-normality
Response is proportionate and concise; does not deliver a lengthy lecture on distributional theory
Does NOT recommend a nonparametric test based solely on the histogram looking non-normal, without considering n or the estimand

evals.prompt: I ran Shapiro-Wilk on my residuals (n=150, OLS regression) and got p = 0.08. So normality isn't violated and my inference is valid, right?
evals.expected_output: Wrong on two levels. First, p = 0.08 is absence of evidence, not evidence of normality — at n=150 the test has limited power to detect moderate violations. A non-rejection means 'we couldn't detect a violation', not 'normality holds'. Second, residual normality barely matters for coefficient inference at n=150 anyway: the CLT governs the sampling distribution of the estimator, not residual normality. The Shapiro-Wilk result is doing no useful work here in either direction.

assertions.text: Does NOT accept p=0.08 on Shapiro-Wilk as confirmation that normality holds or that inference is validated
States that a non-significant Shapiro-Wilk is absence of evidence (low power to detect violations), not positive evidence of normality
Notes that residual normality matters little for coefficient inference at n=150 — the CLT governs the sampling distribution of the estimator
Does NOT endorse the Shapiro-Wilk result as the reason to proceed with inference

evals.prompt: I have two groups, n=45 per group, with moderately right-skewed outcomes (skewness ~1.5). My collaborator says I should use a permutation test instead of a t-test because it's 'safer' for non-normal data. Should I switch?
evals.expected_output: No switch needed. At n=45 with skewness ~1.5, the Berry-Esseen bound is roughly skewness/√n ≈ 1.5/√45 ≈ 0.22 for one sample; the two-sample test is more forgiving because skew partially cancels. The t-test's level is approximately valid here. A permutation test is also valid — but 'safer' implies the t-test is unsafe when it isn't. Both are fine; the t-test is the simpler and appropriate choice for a mean comparison.

assertions.text: States the t-test is approximately valid at n=45 with moderate skew (~1.5), citing CLT or Berry-Esseen reasoning
Does NOT recommend switching to a permutation test as necessary for this case
Does NOT characterize the t-test as unsafe or problematic at this n and skew level
Explains why switching to a permutation test provides no meaningful protection benefit at this n and skew — e.g. asymptotic equivalence, or that the sampling distribution error is already small

evals.prompt: I have a trial with 3 pre-specified primary outcomes. I tested each with a planned t-test and got p-values of 0.04, 0.03, and 0.08. A reviewer says I must apply Bonferroni correction. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: Whether correction is required depends on the analysis plan, field conventions, and the regulatory context — 'must' is too strong. For pre-specified primary outcomes with distinct scientific questions, the case for correction is weaker than for exploratory data-dredging. When correction is warranted, Bonferroni is the most conservative choice: the Holm procedure is uniformly more powerful and also controls FWER; FDR control (Benjamini-Hochberg) is appropriate when false-discovery rate rather than FWER is the right goal. The reviewer has a point about multiplicity; the disagreement is about whether Bonferroni specifically is obligatory.

assertions.text: Does NOT simply endorse 'must apply Bonferroni' without engaging with the pre-specification context
Engages with the pre-specification context — notes it defines the family or reduces data-dredging concerns, rather than treating pre-specification as irrelevant to the multiplicity question
Mentions Holm or another less-conservative alternative to Bonferroni (Holm, FDR/BH, Benjamini-Hochberg) as preferable or more powerful when correction is warranted
Acknowledges the reviewer's multiplicity concern as legitimate — does not dismiss correction entirely
Does NOT say multiple comparisons corrections are never needed

evals.prompt: I want to estimate the causal effect of a new training program on employee performance. I'll compare trained vs untrained employees using a t-test. Participation was voluntary. Is there anything wrong with that approach?
evals.expected_output: Yes — voluntary participation means self-selection into training. The t-test is mechanically valid but it estimates a confounded descriptive contrast, not a causal effect. Employees who choose to train likely differ from those who don't on motivation, tenure, role, and other performance predictors. The estimand issue (confounded descriptive vs causal effect) dominates any distributional concern. To approach causal identification: propensity score methods or matching, difference-in-differences if pre/post data exist, instrumental variable if there's a valid instrument, or regression discontinuity if there's an eligibility threshold. A well-run comparison requires making the ignorability assumption explicit and arguing for it.

assertions.text: Identifies voluntary participation / self-selection as the core problem — the comparison is confounded
Distinguishes the descriptive contrast (t-test gives this) from a causal estimand (which requires handling selection)
Names at least one approach to causal identification given the observational design (e.g. propensity scores, DiD, IV, matching)
Frames the issue as an identification problem, not a distributional/assumption problem
Does NOT accept the t-test as an estimator of the causal effect of training without flagging the confounding

evals.prompt: I'm studying the causal effect of obesity on heart disease risk. I have data on obesity status, age, smoking, and cardiovascular fitness. I included cardiovascular fitness as a covariate in my logistic regression because it seemed like an important variable to control for. Is that the right approach?
evals.expected_output: Identifies that cardiovascular fitness is likely a mediator of obesity on heart disease (obesity → reduced fitness → heart disease), not a confounder. Adjusting for a mediator blocks the causal path and biases the estimate of the total effect. Also notes fitness could be a collider in some DAGs. Recommends thinking about the DAG and whether the estimand is the total effect or the direct effect not through fitness.

assertions.text: Identifies that cardiovascular fitness is plausibly a mediator (on the causal path from obesity to heart disease) rather than a confounder
States that adjusting for a mediator blocks the causal pathway running through it, so the estimate no longer reflects the total causal effect — instead estimating some version of the direct effect
Frames the issue in terms of what estimand is wanted: total effect vs direct effect not through fitness
Does NOT simply endorse including fitness 'because it's important' without discussing its causal role

Notes that adjustment decisions should be guided by causal structure (e.g. DAG, or explicit reasoning about whether variables are confounders vs mediators vs colliders) — not by statistical importance, correlation with the outcome, or model fit

evals.prompt: I measured depression scores before and after a 12-week intervention. My colleague says I should use the change score (post minus pre) as the outcome in a t-test. My advisor says I should use the post-score as the outcome with the pre-score as a covariate (ANCOVA). We're arguing about which is correct. Which one should I use?
evals.expected_output: Explains that this is Lord's paradox / the ANCOVA vs change score debate. They are not testing the same estimand: ANCOVA estimates the treatment effect adjusting for baseline (conditional effect); change score tests mean change without conditioning on baseline level. ANCOVA is more powerful and less biased when baseline predicts outcome (true regression to the mean); change score is unbiased regardless. In a randomized experiment both are unbiased but ANCOVA is more efficient. In observational studies ANCOVA conditions on baseline which can introduce or remove bias depending on design.

assertions.text: Recognizes this as a legitimate estimand question, not merely a procedural preference — the two approaches can give different answers
States that ANCOVA estimates the effect conditional on baseline (adjusting for pre-score) while the change score estimates mean gain without that conditioning
Notes that in a randomized experiment both are unbiased but ANCOVA is more efficient (gains power by explaining baseline variance)

Notes that in observational settings with unequal baseline distributions, neither approach is automatically unbiased — the right choice depends on causal structure and the chosen estimand, not on statistical convention
Does NOT simply declare one approach universally correct without considering the study design

evals.prompt: We selected the 20 worst-performing stores in our chain, rolled out a new training program, and measured performance 3 months later. 17 of 20 stores improved their performance. Our CMO says this is strong evidence the training program works. Is it?
evals.expected_output: Identifies regression to the mean as a major alternative explanation: stores selected for being unusually bad will tend to improve on the next measurement even with no intervention, because extreme values partly reflect random fluctuation. The 17/20 improvement rate could be entirely explained by RTM without any causal effect of training. The correct design is a control group of similarly poor-performing stores that did not receive training, or a pre-registered time-series comparison.

assertions.text: Identifies regression to the mean as the primary alternative explanation — stores selected for being extreme will tend to improve regardless of intervention
Explains the mechanism: extreme observed values partly reflect random error; on remeasurement the random component regresses toward the population mean
States that a control group of similar low-performing stores not receiving training is needed to separate RTM from a true treatment effect
Does NOT validate the 17/20 improvement rate as strong causal evidence without raising RTM
Notes that the design as described (select low performers, treat all, measure again) makes RTM confounding unresolvable without a control group
